title: Monolith vs Microservices
description: Understand the key differences between monolithic and microservices architectures and their trade-offs.

data.text: When building software, one of the first architectural decisions you face is whether to structure your application as a monolith or as microservices. Netflix famously transitioned from a monolithic DVD rental system to microservices to handle its streaming growth, while Amazon moved from a single e-commerce monolith to hundreds of microservices.

A monolithic application is built as a single unified unit. All components—user interface, business logic, and data access—are tightly coupled and deployed together. Examples include traditional .NET Framework applications or Ruby on Rails apps with a single codebase.

data.title: Monolith Characteristics
items: Scaling requires duplicating the entire application
Technology stack is uniform across the system

data.text: Microservices architecture structures an application as a collection of small, autonomous services, each running in its own process and communicating via lightweight mechanisms like HTTP APIs or message queues. Each service is built around a specific business capability and can be deployed independently.

data.title: Real-World Example
data.text: Uber decomposed its original monolith into microservices for ride matching, payments, notifications, and user management, allowing teams to ship features independently at scale.

items.question: Is a monolith always bad?
items.answer: No. Monoliths are simpler to develop, test, and deploy for small teams and early-stage products. Many successful companies started with monoliths.

items.question: Can I mix monoliths and microservices?
items.answer: Yes. Strangler Fig pattern lets you incrementally extract services from a monolith while keeping the system running.

items.question: Does microservices mean micro in size?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Services should be small enough to be owned by one team, but large enough to deliver meaningful business value.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Monoliths are simpler for small teams and early products
Microservices enable independent scaling and deployment
Both architectures have valid use cases
The choice depends on team size, complexity, and growth trajectory
data.takeaway: Start with a monolith if you are unsure; migrate to microservices when scaling demands it.
